newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Shevardnadze to USA seeking help with separatists.
newsitem.headline: Shevardnadze to USA seeking help with separatists.

text.p: Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze left for a state visit to the United States on Wednesday, seeking Western help in dealing with separatists after three years of inconclusive Russian-led peace efforts.
The former Soviet foreign minister will be received at the White House by U.S. President Bill Clinton and at United Nations headquarters in New York by Secretary-General Kofi Annan.
Shevardnadze's aides said he wanted to see what part the United States and United Nations can play in ending Georgia's unsolved conflict with Abkhaz separatists.

"The USA is more actively joining the process of achieving a resolution of the Abkhaz conflict. I have a great hope that a new phase of the resolution of the conflict can begin under the aegis of the U.N.," Shevardnadze said in a Monday radio address.

Georgia lost Abkhazia, a lush subtropical Black Sea region in the northwest of the mountainous republic, when its disorganised military was driven out in 1993 after a year of fighting that killed more than 10,000 people.
Abkhazia remains Shevardnadze's main political headache after three years of Russian-led peace talks with the separatists, who insist on more autonomy than Georgia is willing to tolerate.

In the past, the white-haired Shevardnadze was the toast of Washington for his leading role in helping to end the Cold War. His wide grin broke the stony-faced sterotype of previous Kremlin foreign policy chiefs.
But his return to power in his native Georgia has been far less glamourous.
Abkhazia is one of several ethnic and civil conflicts that have bedevilled the country of six million since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
Shevardnadze, 68, has repeatedly said he would like to see a larger role for the United Nations in Abkhazia, which already has about 150 military observers.

Georgia says a contingent of 1,500 Russian peacekeepers must begin leaving Abkhazia after July 31 if Moscow does not agree that they do more, including patrolling a wider part of the province and helping Georgian refugees resettle.
So far the Russians have refused, saying the Abkhaz should also agree to the new mandate. They are bitterly opposed.
Some Georgian politicians want Western troops to replace the Russians, though most observers say that is not realistic.

Diplomats say few Western leaders would be willing to send peacekeepers to Georgia, which still has Russian military bases and which Moscow continues to see as part of its strategic underbelly, especially with the Kremlin still smarting from NATO's announced expansion.

"They (the Georgians) have been told that there will not be a replacement for the Russians if they leave, and that the West sees the Russian peacekeeping mission as on the whole a success," said a Western diplomat in Tbilisi.
Many say the departure of the Russian peacekeeping force could leave a vacuum and spark new war in Abkhazia.

This could destroy the fragile stability and economic progress that Shevardnadze has carefully woven over the past three years. Georgia currently has the highest rate of economic growth - 10 percent in 1996 and a projected 10-12 per cent in 1997 - of any former Soviet republic.

Shevardnadze, whose plane from Tbilisi was due to land in New York on Wednesday evening, local time, is also scheduled to meet business leaders and officials from the World Bank during the four-day trip.
